claim: Many retroviral Gag proteins contain PPXY late assembly domain motifs that recruit proteins of the NEDD4 E3 ubiquitin ligase family to facilitate virus release.
source: Many retroviral Gag proteins contain PPXY late assembly domain motifs that recruit proteins of the NEDD4 E3 ubiquitin ligase family to facilitate virus release.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about retroviral biology and NEDD4 E3 ubiquitin ligases.

claim: Overexpression of NEDD4L can stimulate HIV-1 release.
source: Overexpression of NEDD4L can also stimulate HIV-1 release but in this case the Gag protein lacks a PPXY motif, suggesting that NEDD4L may function through an adaptor protein.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and is confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: HIV-1 Gag protein lacks a PPXY motif.
source: Overexpression of NEDD4L can also stimulate HIV-1 release but in this case the Gag protein lacks a PPXY motif, suggesting that NEDD4L may function through an adaptor protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 Gag structure.

claim: NEDD4L may function through an adaptor protein in HIV-1 release.
source: Overexpression of NEDD4L can also stimulate HIV-1 release but in this case the Gag protein lacks a PPXY motif, suggesting that NEDD4L may function through an adaptor protein.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that HIV-1 Gag lacks PPXY motifs but NEDD4L still stimulates release.

claim: Angiomotin (AMOT) can bind both NEDD4L and HIV-1 Gag.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the cellular protein Angiomotin (AMOT) can bind both NEDD4L and HIV-1 Gag.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: HIV-1 release is stimulated by AMOT overexpression.
source: HIV-1 release and infectivity are stimulated by AMOT overexpression and inhibited by AMOT depletion, whereas AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: HIV-1 infectivity is stimulated by AMOT overexpression.
source: HIV-1 release and infectivity are stimulated by AMOT overexpression and inhibited by AMOT depletion, whereas AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: HIV-1 release is inhibited by AMOT depletion.
source: HIV-1 release and infectivity are stimulated by AMOT overexpression and inhibited by AMOT depletion, whereas AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 9.

claim: HIV-1 infectivity is inhibited by AMOT depletion.
source: HIV-1 release and infectivity are stimulated by AMOT overexpression and inhibited by AMOT depletion, whereas AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
source: HIV-1 release and infectivity are stimulated by AMOT overexpression and inhibited by AMOT depletion, whereas AMOT mutants that cannot bind NEDD4L cannot function in virus release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In the absence of AMOT, assembling Gag molecules fail to form a fully spherical enveloped particle.
source: Electron microscopic analyses revealed that in the absence of AMOT assembling Gag molecules fail to form a fully spherical enveloped particle.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: AMOT and other motin family members function together with NEDD4L to help complete immature virion assembly prior to ESCRT-mediated virus budding.
source: Our experiments indicate that AMOT and other motin family members function together with NEDD4L to help complete immature virion assembly prior to ESCRT-mediated virus budding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A large number of enveloped viruses, including HIV-1, usurp the cellular ESCRT pathway to bud from cells.
source: As obligate parasites, viruses must harness host cellular pathways to complete many different steps in viral replication. For example, a large number of enveloped viruses, including HIV-1, usurp the cellular ESCRT (Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport) pathway to bud from cells (for recent reviews, see Meng and Lever, 2013; Votteler and Sundquist, 2013; Weissenhorn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Viral structural proteins typically use one or more short peptide motifs, termed 'late assembly domains', to bind and recruit early-acting ESCRT factors or ESCRT-associated E3 ubiquitin ligases to sites of viral assembly and budding.
source: Viral structural proteins typically use one or more short peptide motifs, termed 'late assembly domains', to bind and recruit early-acting ESCRT factors or ESCRT-associated E3 ubiquitin ligases to sites of viral assembly and budding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral assembly mechanisms.

claim: The PTAP motif binds the UEV domain of the TSG101 subunit of the ESCRT-I complex.
source: The three best characterized viral late assembly domains are: (1) the 'PTAP' motif (Pro-Thr/Ser-Ala-Pro), which binds the UEV domain of the TSG101 subunit of the ESCRT-I complex, (2) the 'YPXnL' motif (Tyr-Pro-Xn-Leu, where X can vary in identity and sequence length), which binds the V domain of the ESCRT factor ALIX, and (3) the 'PPXY' motif (Pro-Pro-X-Tyr), which binds the WW domains of NEDD4 family E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral late assembly domains.

claim: The YPXnL motif binds the V domain of the ESCRT factor ALIX.
source: The three best characterized viral late assembly domains are: (1) the 'PTAP' motif (Pro-Thr/Ser-Ala-Pro), which binds the UEV domain of the TSG101 subunit of the ESCRT-I complex, (2) the 'YPXnL' motif (Tyr-Pro-Xn-Leu, where X can vary in identity and sequence length), which binds the V domain of the ESCRT factor ALIX, and (3) the 'PPXY' motif (Pro-Pro-X-Tyr), which binds the WW domains of NEDD4 family E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral late assembly domains.

claim: The PPXY motif binds the WW domains of NEDD4 family E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: The three best characterized viral late assembly domains are: (1) the 'PTAP' motif (Pro-Thr/Ser-Ala-Pro), which binds the UEV domain of the TSG101 subunit of the ESCRT-I complex, (2) the 'YPXnL' motif (Tyr-Pro-Xn-Leu, where X can vary in identity and sequence length), which binds the V domain of the ESCRT factor ALIX, and (3) the 'PPXY' motif (Pro-Pro-X-Tyr), which binds the WW domains of NEDD4 family E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral late assembly domains.

claim: All three viral late assembly domains mimic cellular protein–protein interactions that facilitate ESCRT-dependent vesiculation processes such as multi-vesicular body (MVB) biogenesis and ectosome formation.
source: All three of these viral late assembly domains mimic cellular protein–protein interactions that facilitate ESCRT-dependent vesiculation processes such as multi-vesicular body (MVB) biogenesis and ectosome formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between viral and cellular ESCRT functions.

claim: Efficient release of PIV5 requires a non-canonical 'FPIV' late assembly domain motif.
source: For example, efficient release of the model paramyxovirus, PIV5, requires a non-canonical 'FPIV' late assembly domain motif, ubiquitylation of the matrix (M) protein, and host Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1) (Schmitt et al., 2005; Pei et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Efficient release of PIV5 requires ubiquitylation of the matrix (M) protein.
source: For example, efficient release of the model paramyxovirus, PIV5, requires a non-canonical 'FPIV' late assembly domain motif, ubiquitylation of the matrix (M) protein, and host Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1) (Schmitt et al., 2005; Pei et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Efficient release of PIV5 requires host Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1).
source: For example, efficient release of the model paramyxovirus, PIV5, requires a non-canonical 'FPIV' late assembly domain motif, ubiquitylation of the matrix (M) protein, and host Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1) (Schmitt et al., 2005; Pei et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no evidence that AMOTL1 can bind the FPIV late assembly domain.
source: There is no evidence that AMOTL1 can bind the FPIV late assembly domain, however, and any relationships between ubiquitin, AMOTL1 and the FPIV late assembly domain activity are not yet understood (Pei et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence, supported by a citation.

claim: The C-terminal p6 region of HIV-1 Gag contains canonical PTAP and YPXnL motifs that serve as the major functional late assembly domains in most cell types.
source: The C-terminal p6 region of the viral Gag structural protein contains canonical PTAP and YPXnL motifs that serve as the major functional late assembly domains in most cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 Gag structure and function.

claim: The release of 'crippled' HIV-1 Gag constructs that lack both PTAP and YPXnL late domains can still be stimulated by overexpression of NEDD4L.
source: Nevertheless, the release of 'crippled' HIV-1 Gag constructs that lack both of these late domains can still be stimulated by overexpression of the HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase, NEDD4L (also known as NEDD4-2) (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Humans express nine different NEDD4 protein family members.
source: Humans express nine different NEDD4 protein family members (reviewed in Ingham et al., 2004; Bernassola et al., 2008), but NEDD4L stimulates virus budding more potently than any other NEDD4 family member, implying that HIV-1 Gag preferentially engages this E3 ubiquitin ligase (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: NEDD4L stimulates virus budding more potently than any other NEDD4 family member.
source: Humans express nine different NEDD4 protein family members (reviewed in Ingham et al., 2004; Bernassola et al., 2008), but NEDD4L stimulates virus budding more potently than any other NEDD4 family member, implying that HIV-1 Gag preferentially engages this E3 ubiquitin ligase (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HIV-1 Gag preferentially engages NEDD4L E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Humans express nine different NEDD4 protein family members (reviewed in Ingham et al., 2004; Bernassola et al., 2008), but NEDD4L stimulates virus budding more potently than any other NEDD4 family member, implying that HIV-1 Gag preferentially engages this E3 ubiquitin ligase (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NEDD4L is more potent than other family members.

claim: NEDD4L has many different isoforms.
source: NEDD4L has many different isoforms (Chen et al., 2001; Dunn et al., 2002; Itani et al., 2005), but isoform 2 (also called NEDD4-2s, and here termed NEDD4L) potently stimulates the budding of crippled HIV-1 constructs, and uniquely rescues the Gag processing defects that accompany defective budding (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NEDD4L isoform 2 potently stimulates the budding of crippled HIV-1 constructs.
source: NEDD4L has many different isoforms (Chen et al., 2001; Dunn et al., 2002; Itani et al., 2005), but isoform 2 (also called NEDD4-2s, and here termed NEDD4L) potently stimulates the budding of crippled HIV-1 constructs, and uniquely rescues the Gag processing defects that accompany defective budding (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L isoform 2 uniquely rescues the Gag processing defects that accompany defective budding.
source: NEDD4L has many different isoforms (Chen et al., 2001; Dunn et al., 2002; Itani et al., 2005), but isoform 2 (also called NEDD4-2s, and here termed NEDD4L) potently stimulates the budding of crippled HIV-1 constructs, and uniquely rescues the Gag processing defects that accompany defective budding (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L isoform 2 contains only the final 31 residues of the N-terminal C2 membrane binding domain.
source: This NEDD4L isoform contains only the final 31 residues of the N-terminal C2 membrane binding domain, a central linker region that contains four WW domains, and a C-terminal HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase domain that forms Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains (see Figure 1A) (Kim and Huibregtse, 2009; Weiss et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L isoform 2 contains a central linker region that contains four WW domains.
source: This NEDD4L isoform contains only the final 31 residues of the N-terminal C2 membrane binding domain, a central linker region that contains four WW domains, and a C-terminal HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase domain that forms Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains (see Figure 1A) (Kim and Huibregtse, 2009; Weiss et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L isoform 2 contains a C-terminal HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase domain that forms Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains.
source: This NEDD4L isoform contains only the final 31 residues of the N-terminal C2 membrane binding domain, a central linker region that contains four WW domains, and a C-terminal HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase domain that forms Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains (see Figure 1A) (Kim and Huibregtse, 2009; Weiss et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimulation of HIV-1 budding requires NEDD4L E3 ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: Stimulation of HIV-1 budding requires NEDD4L E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, indicating that Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains perform an essential function (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains perform an essential function in HIV-1 budding.
source: Stimulation of HIV-1 budding requires NEDD4L E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, indicating that Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains perform an essential function (Chung et al., 2008; Usami et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for NEDD4L E3 ligase activity and the fact that NEDD4L forms Lys-63-linked chains.

claim: HIV-1 Gag itself is the leading candidate for the functional target(s) of Lys-63 poly-ubiquitylation.
source: The functional target(s) of Lys-63 poly-ubiquitylation has not been established definitively, but HIV-1 Gag itself is the leading candidate because functional virus budding correlates with Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitylation of Gag, and because NEDD4L truncation constructs that include the HECT domain can be functionally rescued by fusion to the HIV-1 Gag-targeting cyclophilin A domain (Weiss et al., 2010; Sette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on correlative evidence and functional rescue experiments cited from previous studies.

claim: Functional virus budding correlates with Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitylation of Gag.
source: The functional target(s) of Lys-63 poly-ubiquitylation has not been established definitively, but HIV-1 Gag itself is the leading candidate because functional virus budding correlates with Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitylation of Gag, and because NEDD4L truncation constructs that include the HECT domain can be functionally rescued by fusion to the HIV-1 Gag-targeting cyclophilin A domain (Weiss et al., 2010; Sette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L truncation constructs that include the HECT domain can be functionally rescued by fusion to the HIV-1 Gag-targeting cyclophilin A domain.
source: The functional target(s) of Lys-63 poly-ubiquitylation has not been established definitively, but HIV-1 Gag itself is the leading candidate because functional virus budding correlates with Lys-63-linked poly-ubiquitylation of Gag, and because NEDD4L truncation constructs that include the HECT domain can be functionally rescued by fusion to the HIV-1 Gag-targeting cyclophilin A domain (Weiss et al., 2010; Sette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HIV-1 Gag lacks identifiable PPXY motifs.
source: HIV-1 Gag lacks identifiable PPXY motifs, however, and there is no evidence that Gag can bind NEDD4L directly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 Gag structure.

claim: There is no evidence that HIV-1 Gag can bind NEDD4L directly.
source: HIV-1 Gag lacks identifiable PPXY motifs, however, and there is no evidence that Gag can bind NEDD4L directly.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence in the literature prior to this study.

claim: AMOT p130 was identified as a protein that co-purified with OSF-NEDD4L in affinity purification/mass spectrometry experiments.
source: The p130 isoform of human Angiomotin was unambiguously identified as a protein that co-purified with OSF-NEDD4L in three independent repetitions of this experiment, (lane 2, labeled AMOT p130, peptide coverage data are summarized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Smaller AMOT p130 fragments were identified in affinity purification experiments with OSF-NEDD4L.
source: Smaller AMOT p130 fragments were also identified, as was the related AMOT family protein, Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the affinity purification experiments.

claim: AMOTL1 was identified in affinity purification experiments with OSF-NEDD4L.
source: Smaller AMOT p130 fragments were also identified, as was the related AMOT family protein, Angiomotin-like protein 1 (AMOTL1, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the affinity purification experiments.

claim: Cells express two AMOT isoforms: a longer p130 isoform and a shorter C-terminal p80 isoform.
source: Cells express two AMOT isoforms, a longer p130 isoform, and a shorter C-terminal p80 isoform that is expressed from an alternatively spliced message (Figure 1A) (Moreau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AMOT p80 is expressed from an alternatively spliced message.
source: Cells express two AMOT isoforms, a longer p130 isoform, and a shorter C-terminal p80 isoform that is expressed from an alternatively spliced message (Figure 1A) (Moreau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: AMOT p130 binds NEDD4 protein family members via interactions between the four central NEDD4 WW domains and three PPXY motifs located within the N-terminal extension that is unique to the AMOT p130 isoform.
source: AMOT p130 binds NEDD4 protein family members via interactions between the four central NEDD4 WW domains and three PPXY motifs located within the N-terminal extension that is unique to the AMOT p130 isoform (Figure 1A) (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AMOT p130 co-immunoprecipitated with exogenously expressed OSF-NEDD4L.
source: In good agreement with this report and with our affinity purification/mass spectrometry results, we found that AMOT p130 co-immunoprecipitated with exogenously expressed OSF-NEDD4L (Figure 1C, panel 1, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AMOT p130 did not co-immunoprecipitate with a mutant OSF-NEDD4L protein that contained inactivating Trp to Ala substitutions in the key PPXY-binding residues from each of the four WW domains.
source: In contrast, AMOT p130 did not co-immunoprecipitate with a mutant OSF-NEDD4L protein that contained inactivating Trp to Ala substitutions in the key PPXY-binding 'W39' residues from each of the four WW domains (denoted OSF-NEDD4LΔWW, panel 1, compare lanes 2 and 3) (Otte et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and a citation describing the mutations.

claim: NEDD4 proteins can ubiquitylate and reduce AMOT p130 levels.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that NEDD4 proteins can ubiquitylate and reduce AMOT p130 levels (Wang et al., 2012), and we also observed that OSF-NEDD4L overexpression modestly reduced AMOT p130 levels (Figure 1C, panel 3, compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: OSF-NEDD4L overexpression modestly reduced AMOT p130 levels.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that NEDD4 proteins can ubiquitylate and reduce AMOT p130 levels (Wang et al., 2012), and we also observed that OSF-NEDD4L overexpression modestly reduced AMOT p130 levels (Figure 1C, panel 3, compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AMOT p130 co-immunoprecipitated with OSF-NEDD4L proteins carrying an inactivating Cys942Ala point mutation in the active site cysteine of the HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase domain.
source: Once again, AMOT p130 (and breakdown products) co-immunoprecipitated with OSF-NEDD4LC942A (panel 1, lane 4), but not with a protein that also contained inactivating WW domain mutations (OSF-NEDD4LΔWW/C942A panel 1, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AMOT p130 did not co-immunoprecipitate with OSF-NEDD4L that contained both inactivating WW domain mutations and an inactivating HECT domain mutation.
source: Once again, AMOT p130 (and breakdown products) co-immunoprecipitated with OSF-NEDD4LC942A (panel 1, lane 4), but not with a protein that also contained inactivating WW domain mutations (OSF-NEDD4LΔWW/C942A panel 1, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Cys942Ala mutation in NEDD4L increased OSF-NEDD4L levels in the lysate and immunoprecipitate.
source: This mutation increased OSF-NEDD4L levels in the lysate and immunoprecipitate (panels 2 and 4 compare lanes 4 and 5 to lanes 2 and 3) and restored normal AMOT protein levels (panel 3, compare lanes 4, 5 and 1 to lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Cys942Ala mutation in NEDD4L restored normal AMOT protein levels.
source: This mutation increased OSF-NEDD4L levels in the lysate and immunoprecipitate (panels 2 and 4 compare lanes 4 and 5 to lanes 2 and 3) and restored normal AMOT protein levels (panel 3, compare lanes 4, 5 and 1 to lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AMOT p130 co-precipitation levels were higher with OSF-NEDD4LC942A than with wild type OSF-NEDD4L.
source: AMOT p130 co-precipitation levels were higher with OSF-NEDD4LC942A than with wild type OSF-NEDD4L, presumably owing to the higher cellular levels of both OSF-NEDD4L and AMOT p130 (compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutating the three N-terminal AMOT p130 PPXY motifs strongly inhibited co-immunoprecipitation of HA-AMOT p130 with OSF-NEDD4L.
source: Firstly, mutating the three N-terminal AMOT p130 PPXY motifs strongly inhibited co-immunoprecipitation of HA-AMOT p130 with OSF-NEDD4L (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel 1, compare lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Endogenous AMOT p80 failed to co-immunoprecipitate with either OSF-NEDD4L or OSF-NEDD4LC942A.
source: Secondly, endogenous AMOT p80, which lacks the N-terminal PPXY motifs, failed to co-immunoprecipitate with either OSF-NEDD4L or OSF-NEDD4LC942A (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 2 and 4), even though AMOT p80 was present in the 293T cell extracts (panel 3, lanes 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exogenously expressed, epitope-tagged NEDD4L and AMOT p130 co-localized well in HeLa-M cells.
source: Thirdly, we observed that exogenously expressed, epitope-tagged NEDD4L and AMOT p130 co-localized well in HeLa-M cells, and this co-localization required both the AMOT PPXY and NEDD4L WW motifs (data not shown), in good agreement with previous reports that motins co-localize with other NEDD4 family members (Skouloudaki and Walz, 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: Co-localization of NEDD4L and AMOT p130 in HeLa-M cells required both the AMOT PPXY and NEDD4L WW motifs.
source: Thirdly, we observed that exogenously expressed, epitope-tagged NEDD4L and AMOT p130 co-localized well in HeLa-M cells, and this co-localization required both the AMOT PPXY and NEDD4L WW motifs (data not shown), in good agreement with previous reports that motins co-localize with other NEDD4 family members (Skouloudaki and Walz, 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: NEDD4L interacts specifically with AMOT p130 in cells.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that NEDD4L interacts specifically with AMOT p130 in cells and that the interaction requires the WW domains of NEDD4L and the PPXY motifs of AMOT.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: The interaction between NEDD4L and AMOT p130 requires the WW domains of NEDD4L and the PPXY motifs of AMOT.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that NEDD4L interacts specifically with AMOT p130 in cells and that the interaction requires the WW domains of NEDD4L and the PPXY motifs of AMOT.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: AMOT p130 binds NEDD4L directly.
source: Wild type and mutant NEDD4L proteins and an HIV-1 Gag protein that lacked the flexible p6 domain (GagΔp6) were expressed in Escherichia coli and purified to near homogeneity (Figure 2A, lanes 1 and 2, and Figure 2B, lane 1, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down experiments with purified recombinant proteins shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NEDD4L did not bind an immobilized control OSF-GFP protein.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, NEDD4L did not bind an immobilized control OSF-GFP protein, but bound with at least 1:1 stoichiometry to immobilized OSF-AMOT p130 (compare lanes 4 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NEDD4L bound with at least 1:1 stoichiometry to immobilized OSF-AMOT p130.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, NEDD4L did not bind an immobilized control OSF-GFP protein, but bound with at least 1:1 stoichiometry to immobilized OSF-AMOT p130 (compare lanes 4 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Binding of the NEDD4LΔWW mutant protein to AMOT p130 was nearly undetectable.
source: In contrast, binding of the NEDD4LΔWW mutant protein was nearly undetectable (Figure 2A, compare lanes 7 and 8, particularly in the western blot in panel 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NEDD4L and AMOT p130 bind one another directly, with the WW domains of NEDD4L binding the PPXY motifs of AMOT p130.
source: These experiments confirm that NEDD4L and AMOT p130 bind one another directly, with the WW domains of NEDD4L binding the PPXY motifs of AMOT p130.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIV-1 GagΔp6 bound immobilized OSF-AMOT p130.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, HIV-1 GagΔp6 bound immobilized OSF-AMOT p130, but did not bind an immobilized OSF-GFP control (compare lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HIV-1 GagΔp6 did not bind an immobilized OSF-GFP control.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, HIV-1 GagΔp6 bound immobilized OSF-AMOT p130, but did not bind an immobilized OSF-GFP control (compare lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction between AMOT p130 and GagΔp6 does not appear to be mediated by nucleic acids.
source: This interaction did not appear to be mediated by nucleic acids because the affinity-purified OSF-AMOT p130 protein was pre-washed with high salt solution to remove any bound nucleic acid (see 'Materials and methods'), and because the interaction was maintained, albeit at slightly lower levels, even when immobilized OSF-AMOT p130 was incubated with high concentrations of RNase that were sufficient to eliminate other RNA-mediated Gag-protein interactions (not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental controls performed during the pull-down experiments.

claim: GagΔp6 and NEDD4L appeared to bind OSF-AMOT p130 independently.
source: GagΔp6 and NEDD4L appeared to bind OSF-AMOT p130 independently because their binding levels did not change significantly when all three proteins were incubated together (compare lanes 8 and 9 to lane 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AMOTL1 shares 52% pair-wise sequence identity with AMOT p130.
source: AMOTL1 and AMOTL2 share 52% and 45% pair-wise sequence identity with AMOT p130, and both contain the N-terminal extension and PPXY motifs that are present in AMOT p130 but absent in AMOT p80 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the motin family protein sequences, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AMOTL2 shares 45% pair-wise sequence identity with AMOT p130.
source: AMOTL1 and AMOTL2 share 52% and 45% pair-wise sequence identity with AMOT p130, and both contain the N-terminal extension and PPXY motifs that are present in AMOT p130 but absent in AMOT p80 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the motin family protein sequences, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AMOTL1 and AMOTL2 both contain the N-terminal extension and PPXY motifs that are present in AMOT p130 but absent in AMOT p80.

claim: AMOT p130 is recruited at the half-moon stage of HIV-1 assembly, perhaps by binding cooperatively to Gag and to appropriately curved membranes.
